newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-president renews terror charge against Iran.
newsitem.headline: Ex-president renews terror charge against Iran.

text.p: Former Iranian president Abolhassan Banisadr said he would prove to a Berlin court on Thursday that Iran's religious leader was responsible for the killing of exiled Iranian Kurdish leaders in Berlin in 1992.

Banisadr had already strained relations between Germany and Iran in two days of testimony last month when he accused spiritual leader Ali Khamenei of ordering the assassination, and President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani of approving it.
The ex-president on Thursday resumed his testimony amid tight security in the court trying three Lebanese and one Iranian, alleged ringleader Kazem Darabi, for murder in connection with the killings.

Banisadr, an enemy of Tehran since he was ousted and fled in 1981, told German Radio: "I will present documents showing that all ministers and parliamentary deputies in Iran are obliged by law to obey the spiritual leader, that is Khamenei."
German prosecutors have already angered Iran by issuing an arrest warrant against Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan last March on suspicion of sending out agents to kill the dissidents.
Banisadr said last month that a "council for special operations", including Fallahiyan, Khamenei and four others, was responsible for determining who would be assassinated and how.
"If Fallahiyan carried out this terrorist act, he must have been obeying the spiritual leader, as the law requires."

Two masked men armed with machineguns burst into the restaurant in Berlin on September 17, 1992 and fired at dozens of Iranian dissidents seated at a table. Three leaders of the Iranian Democratic Party of Kurdistan (DPK-I) and their translator were killed.
Despite living in exile in France since 1981, Banisadr, one of the architects of the Islamic revolution against the Shah, says he still has sources inside Iran's government apparatus.
"I am an economist, a sociologist and I do research on Islam. Every day I receive new information. If anyone knows Iran, I do," he told German Radio.

Tehran has asked Germany to extradite Banisadr for allegedly hijacking the military aircraft which he commandeered to flee Iran in 1981. But France has granted Banisadr political asylum, and German authorities have made no move against him.
Iran denies involvement in the assassinations and dismisses Banisadr's testimony as the attempted revenge of an avowed enemy of the government.
It has urged German authorities to disregard Banisadr's statements and said they could damage bilateral relations.
